hops.afterHeading: More columns, not a thicker cortex
hops.title: The microcephaly gene that mice shrugged off
hops.text: Mutations in ASPM are the most common known cause of recessive primary microcephaly. In an MRI study of seven patients, nearly every cortical region had half or less of the usual surface area, the kind of loss the radial unit model predicts. Mice refused to cooperate. Aspm knockout mice had brains only about 10 percent lighter, with no clear loss of cortical area. In 2018, Matthew Johnson, Christopher Walsh, Byoung-Il Bae and colleagues made the same knockout in ferrets, whose larger cortex folds. The ferret brains came out 25 to 40 percent lighter, with smaller cortical surface area and no clear change in thickness where it was measured.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A curious ferret peeking over a lab bench beside a calm white mouse and two plain clay brain models, one smooth and one folded.
image.caption: Aspm loss reduced cortical area in ferrets, with no clear area loss in the mice tested.

hops.title: Outer radial glia behavior in a brain cancer
hops.text: Ten years after filming outer radial glia in fetal cortex, Arnold Kriegstein's group found their likeness in brain cancer. In 2020, Aparna Bhaduri, Kriegstein and colleagues profiled single cells from glioblastoma, a serious brain tumor, and matched them to developing brain maps. Among its stem cells was an invasive population resembling fetal outer radial glia. Filmed live after removal from fresh tumors, these cells moved the cell body along their own fibre before dividing, the same jump seen in developing cortex. In culture, reducing the protein PTPRZ1 in cells from a patient-derived glioblastoma line shortened the jump and reduced invasion, suggesting these cells may reuse a developmental program.

sources.citation: Bhaduri et al., Cell Stem Cell 26:48 (2020)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A glowing round glass dish on a microscope stage showing golden-green cells with rounded bodies and their own thin extensions.
image.caption: Some glioblastoma stem cells resemble fetal outer radial glia, down to the pre-division jump along a fibre.

hops.afterHeading: Taking longer: development on a slower clock
hops.title: The brain does not finish at twenty-five
hops.text: Many people have heard that the brain finishes developing at twenty-five. The data tell a messier story. In 2022, Richard Bethlehem and colleagues pooled 123,984 MRI scans from 101,457 people, ranging from before birth to age 100, and charted how each feature of the brain changes with age. Different features peak at different ages. Average cortical thickness peaks at about 1.7 years. Total cortical surface area peaks near 11. White matter volume, the brain's long-range wiring, keeps rising until about 29. None of those peaks falls at twenty-five.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A frosted birthday cake with plain lit candles beside a potted sapling still sprouting new leaves on a wooden table.
image.caption: Different human brain features peak at different ages, from toddlerhood to nearly thirty.
